book.title: How to Know a Person
book.subtitle: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen
book.edition: First edition, hardcover, Random House, October 24, 2023, 320 pages (publisher page). UK: Allen Lane 2023; Penguin Books paperback 2025, ISBN 9781802064308. Page references below follow the US hardcover pagination as given in a church discussion guide; the UK paperback contents page shows the same chapter start pages.
book.author_credibility: David Brooks is a long-time New York Times opinion columnist (and, per his publisher, a writer for The Atlantic and regular PBS NewsHour commentator) and author of several books on character and social life (The Social Animal, The Road to Character, The Second Mountain). He is not a psychologist or researcher; the book is a synthesis of psychology, philosophy, literature and personal experience. He says he wrote it partly to fix his own reserved, emotionally distant habits, which makes it personal and motivational but also means some advice reflects his temperament and moral outlook more than tested method.
book.evidence_base: Mixed. Some passages lean on peer-reviewed work: William Ickes on empathic accuracy and Nicholas Epley on the 'lesser minds' problem (both in the opening chapters, confirmed in the publisher sample), Dan McAdams's life-story interviews (Chapter 15), Big Five personality research and a 2022 review by Brent Roberts and Hee J. Yoon on personality change (Chapter 13), and developmental psychology for the life-tasks chapter (Erikson; summaries also name Robert Kegan). Much of the practical advice (Illuminators versus Diminishers, accompaniment, the Good Talks tips including looping and loud listening, the hard-conversations tools) comes from essays, philosophers such as Simone Weil and Iris Murdoch, practitioners, interviews and Brooks's own experience. The chapter on a friend in despair rests largely on one case, his friend Peter Marks, who died by suicide after years of depression. Reviewers find it engaging and practical but in places anecdotal.

insights.name: Illuminators versus Diminishers
insights.explanation: Brooks sorts people by the effect they have on others. Diminishers leave you feeling unseen: they steer talk back to themselves, label you quickly, treat you as a means to an end, or simply overlook what you are trying to say. Illuminators leave you feeling bigger and more understood: they are curious, ask follow-up questions, and try to see the world a little from your side. His central claim is that illuminating is a learnable set of skills rather than a personality trait, and that most of us drift into diminishing out of habit, distraction or self-focus rather than malice.
insights.when_to_use: As a quick self-check before and after any conversation that matters: a one-on-one with a report, a first date, dinner with a parent, a networking coffee. Ask afterward: did the other person leave feeling more seen or less seen?
insights.worked_example: After a team lunch, a manager realizes she spent most of it describing her own weekend and answering emails under the table, while a new analyst tried twice to mention a project idea. At the next lunch she sets her phone face down, asks the analyst what drew her to the role, and follows up on the project idea with two specific questions. Same lunch, same people; the difference is whether she was diminishing or illuminating.
common_mistakes: Using the labels to judge others rather than to audit your own behavior.
Assuming warmth alone makes you an illuminator; Brooks stresses that good intentions without listening and questioning skills still leave people unseen.
Performing interest (nodding while waiting to talk) instead of actually being curious.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1 'I See You': Chapter 1 'The Power of Being Seen' (Illuminators and Diminishers defined, pp. 12 to 14, with the Bell Labs story of Harry Nyquist as an Illuminator); Chapter 2 'How Not to See a Person' (Diminisher habits: the quick size-up, egotism, anxiety, naive realism, the lesser-minds problem, objectivism, essentialism, the static mindset, pp. 20 to 22); Chapter 3 'Illumination' (Illuminator qualities: tenderness, receptivity, active curiosity, affection, generosity, a holistic attitude, pp. 32 to 35). Also NYT essay 'The Essential Skills for Being Human' (Oct 19, 2023).
source.underlying_research: The typology is Brooks's own. Chapter 1 supports the claim that we read others poorly with William Ickes's empathic-accuracy research, and Chapter 2 cites Nicholas Epley on the lesser-minds problem. The 54 percent figure (Americans who say nobody knows them well) is confirmed from Brooks's own interview remarks; the underlying survey was not identified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book text (publisher sample, Chapter 1). Memorable and practically useful as a reflective lens, but it is an essayist's typology, not a validated construct; the term echoes Liz Wiseman's practitioner framing 'Multipliers versus Diminishers'. Rated Low on evidence, not on usefulness.

insights.name: Accompaniment: walk beside, do not steer
insights.explanation: Before deep knowing comes ordinary companionship: spending unhurried time alongside someone without an agenda to fix, impress or extract. Brooks names four qualities of good accompaniment: patience (trust builds slowly, so you hold back and respect the other person's timetable, which he links to Simone Weil's idea of 'negative effort'), playfulness (shared activity where being together matters more than the content), other-centeredness (turning down your own self-importance so the other person can be fully themselves), and presence (simply being there, especially in hard times). Talking regularly about small things is what makes it possible to talk about big things later.
insights.when_to_use: Early in any relationship, when someone is going through a hard stretch but is not ready to talk, with teenagers or reserved colleagues, and when rebuilding distance in a family relationship.
insights.worked_example: A father wants to know what is going on with his quiet 15-year-old. Instead of a sit-down talk, he starts driving her to practice and stopping for food afterward, keeping it light. Weeks later, on one of those drives, she brings up a friendship falling apart. At work, a team lead does something similar with a guarded new hire: regular coffee walks with no agenda, which later make a frank conversation about workload possible.
common_mistakes: Treating time together as a setup for the 'real' talk and pushing for disclosure too soon.
Confusing presence with passivity; accompaniment still involves attention and small gestures.
Filling every silence instead of letting the other person set the pace.
situations: Building trust with a guarded new hire
Supporting a friend who will not talk yet

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, Chapter 4 'Accompaniment' (pp. 43 to 54): patience p. 46, playfulness p. 47, other-centeredness p. 50, presence p. 52.
source.underlying_research: Philosophical rather than empirical: Simone Weil's 'negative effort' (confirmed via a blog quoting the chapter). No empirical study identified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Chapter and its four qualities confirmed with page references in a discussion guide; the Weil link confirmed via a blog quoting the book. Support is philosophical and anecdotal. Plausible and consistent with common relationship wisdom, but not tested as stated.

insights.name: Attention is a switch, not a dimmer (be a loud listener)
insights.explanation: Brooks argues that half-attention is visible and diminishing, so attention should be all on or deliberately off: an on/off switch, not a dimmer. When you listen, make it obvious, or as he puts it, be a loud listener: an active, responsive face and body, small verbal encouragements, and follow-up questions that show you tracked what was said, because passive listening nudges speakers toward holding back. He mentions the SLANT routine (sit up, lean forward, ask questions, nod, track the speaker), crediting it only to 'some experts'. He also advises not fearing the pause and framing your reply after the other person finishes.
insights.when_to_use: Any conversation where the other person is telling you something that matters to them: a report raising a concern, a partner describing a bad day, a client explaining a problem, a video call where cues are weaker.
insights.worked_example: On a video call, an engineer explains why a deadline slipped. Her manager closes his other tabs, keeps his camera on, nods visibly, says 'okay, so the vendor API changed' at a natural pause, and asks what she would need to recover. At home that evening, when his partner starts describing a conflict with her sister, he puts his phone in another room before answering rather than half-listening from the couch.
common_mistakes: Multitasking while saying 'go on, I'm listening'.
Over-performing (constant nodding, exaggerated reactions) so it feels like technique rather than interest.
Planning your response while they are still talking.
steps: Decide: can I give full attention right now? If not, say so and set a time.
Remove the obvious competitors: phone, other tabs, notifications.
Show tracking physically: face them, lean in slightly, keep eye contact natural.
Give small verbal signals and brief recaps at natural pauses.
Wait until they finish the point before forming your reply; then ask one follow-up question about what they said.
situations: Report raising a concern in a one-on-one

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, Chapter 6 'Good Talks': attention as on/off switch (p. 74), be a loud listener (p. 75), don't fear the pause (p. 77). Also in the NYT essay 'The Essential Skills for Being Human' (Oct 19, 2023).
source.underlying_research: No study named. Brooks introduces SLANT as a method 'some experts' use, without naming a source (per a blog quoting the book). SLANT is a classroom engagement routine widely associated with Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion and charter-school practice; Brooks does not credit Lemov as far as could be verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via two discussion guides with page references and a review of a Brooks talk. Brooks's support is experiential, but the general point that visibly attentive, responsive listening makes speakers feel understood is consistent with broader listening research not cited here. SLANT is a practitioner tool, not a tested conversational intervention.

insights.name: Deep talk is less awkward than you fear
insights.explanation: People systematically expect deeper conversations with strangers or acquaintances to be more awkward and less enjoyable than they turn out to be, largely because they underestimate how interested the other person is in going deeper. In experiments by Kardas, Kumar and Epley, people who discussed meaningful questions with a stranger reported more connection and less awkwardness than predicted, and many who expected to prefer small talk ended up preferring the deeper conversation. Brooks uses this to argue that our reluctance to ask real questions is a forecasting error, not a sign the other person wants to stay shallow.
insights.when_to_use: When you notice yourself defaulting to weather and weekend plans with someone you would like to know better: a colleague you sit near, a new neighbor, a partner's friend at a party, a mentor.
insights.worked_example: At a conference dinner, a product manager is seated next to a stranger from another company. Instead of only trading job titles, she asks what has surprised him most about his field lately, and later what he would do if he were starting his career over. The conversation runs long, and they exchange contacts. Later she uses the same nudge with her brother-in-law, whom she has only ever discussed sports with, and learns he is quietly thinking about leaving his job.
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to intensely personal topics with no warm-up or consent; the research involved questions both parties answered.
Treating the finding as license to interrogate; reciprocity (you share too) matters.
Assuming everyone in every setting wants depth; read cues and offer an easy exit.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 15 'Life Stories' (reader notes record that people misjudge how much they will enjoy conversation and how willing others are to talk); Chapter 7 'The Right Questions' makes the related point that people are too shy about asking, not too prying.
source.underlying_research: Kardas, M., Kumar, A., and Epley, N. (2022). Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3), 367 to 398. doi:10.1037/pspa0000281. Abstract read: strangers' conversations felt less awkward and more connecting than expected, the gap was largest for deep conversations, and it arose because people underestimated how much partners cared about their disclosures (experiments labeled 1a to 7b; the press-release figure of twelve experiments with more than 1,800 participants was not re-confirmed). Related: Epley and Schroeder (2014) on talking to strangers. Brooks names Epley in the book; whether his endnotes cite this specific paper was not verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Multi-experiment paper in a top journal with consistent effects (abstract confirmed), plus convergent findings on talking to strangers. Caveats: one lab group, mostly structured stranger pairings, and people predicted close-other conversations accurately, so the effect is about acquaintances and strangers. The idea is in the book (Chapter 15); the exact citation is not confirmed.

insights.name: Ask big, open questions (crossroads questions)
insights.explanation: Brooks recommends questions that are specific but open-ended, and big questions that lift people out of their daily routine so they see their life from a distance. His examples include what crossroads someone is at, what the current chapter of their life is about if the next five years were a chapter, and what they would do if they were not afraid. He warns against closed questions and evaluating questions that signal you are about to judge (where did you go to college), and suggests simple prompts such as asking what happened next. Elsewhere he suggests asking how someone came to believe something rather than what they believe. Good questions hand the other person control of the conversation and make them the author of their story, not a witness answering a quiz.
insights.when_to_use: When a conversation is stuck at status updates; in mentoring, career conversations, reunions with old friends, long car rides with a partner, or first dates past the logistics stage.
insights.worked_example: In a quarterly career chat, instead of asking a senior engineer 'Are you happy here?', a manager asks 'What crossroads do you feel like you are at right now?' The engineer talks about wanting to try leading people but fearing losing hands-on work, which reshapes the development plan. On a weekend walk, the same manager asks an old college friend how she came to believe that moving back home was the right call, and hears a story about her mother's health she had never shared.
common_mistakes: Asking big questions cold, before any rapport or context, so they feel like a therapy intake.
Asking a closed version ('Are you happy?') that ends with yes or no.
Firing several big questions in a row without following up on the answer.
Not being willing to answer the same question yourself.
steps: Warm up with ordinary talk and accompaniment first.
Pick one open, specific question that invites reflection (crossroads, next chapter, how did you come to believe that).
Listen to the full answer, then ask a follow-up about the most alive detail.
Offer your own answer if it fits, keeping it brief so the focus stays on them.
Let it go if they deflect; offer the question again another time.
situations: Career conversation with a direct report
Catching up with an old friend

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 7 'The Right Questions' (pp. 82 to 96); 'make them authors, not witnesses' in Chapter 6 (p. 76); 'how did you come to believe' in Chapter 15. Big-question examples also in the NYT essay (Oct 19, 2023) and in his public talks.
source.underlying_research: Indirect support from Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2022) on deeper conversation. Huang et al. (2017) on follow-up questions and liking is often cited in this area, but is not confirmed as cited by Brooks.

insights.confidence_rationale: Question examples now confirmed in three independent sources (NYT essay commentary, Sivers's notes, a review of a Brooks talk). The general direction (open, deeper questions build connection) has research support, but the specific wordings are Brooks's recommendations and have not been tested as such.

insights.name: Perspective getting beats perspective taking
insights.explanation: Trying to imagine yourself in someone else's shoes feels insightful but often does not make you more accurate about what they think or feel, and can make you more confident in a wrong guess. In a large set of experiments, Eyal, Steffel and Epley found that perspective taking did not reliably improve accuracy, while directly getting the other person's perspective (asking and listening) did. Brooks uses this to argue that knowing a person depends on asking and receiving, not on clever inference.
insights.when_to_use: Whenever you catch yourself thinking 'I know what they're thinking': predicting how a stakeholder will react, guessing why a partner is upset, assuming what a customer wants, planning a gift or surprise.
insights.worked_example: A director is sure her peer opposes a reorganization because he wants to protect his headcount. Before a tense meeting she asks him directly what worries him about the plan. His actual concern is that one client would lose its contact person mid-renewal, which is easy to solve. At home, rather than assuming his wife is annoyed about the in-law visit, a husband asks what part of the weekend she is dreading, and learns it is only the airport pickup.
common_mistakes: Treating empathic imagination as a substitute for asking.
Asking in a leading way that confirms your guess ('You're upset about the budget, right?').
Asking once and not checking back as circumstances change.
situations: Figuring out why a partner is upset

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023). Brooks cites Nicholas Epley in Chapter 2 on the lesser-minds problem (confirmed in the publisher sample), and in the NYT essay advises asking about someone's view several times in different ways. Whether the book cites the perspective-getting study itself was not confirmed.
source.underlying_research: Eyal, T., Steffel, M., and Epley, N. (2018). Perspective mistaking: Accurately understanding the mind of another requires getting perspective, not taking perspective. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(4), 547 to 571. doi:10.1037/pspa0000115. 25 experiments; the abstract reports no consistent accuracy gain from perspective taking (if anything a decrease, sometimes with higher confidence), reduced egocentrism, and a final experiment where getting perspective through conversation increased accuracy. The paper does not state a single total sample in its abstract; its main analysis of Experiments 1 to 15 alone covers 1,103 participants. The secondary figure of about 2,600 total remains unconfirmed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Research rating High: 25 experiments in a top journal with a consistent pattern (abstract and paper read). Caveats: tasks were specific (emotion from faces and postures, fake smiles, lie detection, a spouse's preferences), and perspective taking does reduce egocentrism. Flagged because the link to this book is not confirmed: Brooks cites Epley on related points, and his own empathy chapter actually describes mentalizing as projecting your own experience, which this research suggests should be checked by asking.

insights.name: Looping: say it back and check
insights.explanation: Looping means paraphrasing what the other person said and asking whether you got it right, then letting them correct you until they confirm. Brooks says you will be surprised how often you did not actually understand what someone just told you, and that looping also shows you are listening. Summaries report he cautions that doing it mechanically can feel unnatural, so a lighter paraphrase often works as well.
insights.when_to_use: In disagreements, emotionally loaded conversations, when receiving feedback, clarifying requirements, and any moment where the cost of misunderstanding is high. Also useful in writing: restating a request at the top of a reply email before answering.
insights.worked_example: A client says the new dashboard is 'not usable'. Instead of defending it, the account lead says: 'So what I'm hearing is the data is fine, but your team can't find the weekly numbers quickly enough. Is that right?' The client corrects her: it is the filters, not navigation. In a different setting, a woman whose mother says 'You never call' loops back: 'It sounds like you feel I only reach out when I need something?' Her mother says no, she just misses hearing about the kids, which turns an argument into a plan for a weekly call.
common_mistakes: Parroting the exact words, which sounds robotic or patronizing.
Sneaking in your own interpretation or rebuttal inside the paraphrase.
Looping every sentence in a casual chat, which slows things down for no gain.
Skipping the check question, so you never learn you got it wrong.
steps: Listen to the full point before responding.
Restate the core of it in your own words, including any feeling you heard.
Ask a check question: did I get that right, or what did I miss?
Accept correction without defending your version and loop again.
Only once they confirm, give your response.
situations: Argument with a parent or partner

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, Chapter 6 'Good Talks', 'Do the looping' (p. 78); also in the NYT essay 'The Essential Skills for Being Human' (Oct 19, 2023).
source.underlying_research: Practitioner technique from mediation (associated with Gary Friedman and Jack Himmelstein, and popularized by Amanda Ripley's High Conflict). None of the sources read show Brooks crediting a named originator; summaries describe it only as a practice psychologists or experts use. Research on high-quality listening (for example Itzchakov and Kluger) is not confirmed as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book (Chapter 6, p. 78) and the NYT adaptation. Widely used by trained mediators and consistent with research on reflective listening, but Brooks's treatment is short and the step format here is synthesized. Attribution in the book is unverified.

insights.name: Conversation as joint exploration (be a midwife, not a lecturer)
insights.explanation: Brooks defines a good conversation as joint exploration rather than people making statements at each other: someone floats a half-formed idea, the other person grabs its core, adds their own angle and hands it back, and the talk ends somewhere neither started. He offers a midwife model, where your role is to help the other person bring out their own thinking. In disagreements he suggests keeping the shared core value at the center and looking for the deeper disagreement beneath the surface one. And he warns against topping: answering someone's story with a bigger one of your own.
insights.when_to_use: Brainstorms, coaching conversations, dinner-table debates, helping a friend think through a decision, discussing politics or values with someone who disagrees.
insights.worked_example: A friend is torn about whether to take a job in another city. Instead of listing pros and cons from his own experience, the listener asks what parts of the new job she keeps thinking about, then builds on her answer: 'You said you light up talking about the team, what would you miss here?' She reaches her own decision. In a work planning session, a team lead uses the same approach with a junior colleague's half-formed idea, asking what problem it solves first instead of critiquing it.
common_mistakes: Topping: answering someone's story with a bigger one of your own.
Turning the exchange into a debate to win.
Steering toward the conclusion you already hold while pretending to explore.
situations: Helping a friend with a big decision

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 6 'Good Talks': joint exploration (p. 73), midwife model (p. 79), keep the gem statement at the center and find the disagreement under the disagreement (p. 80), don't be a topper (p. 81).
source.underlying_research: No specific study identified; draws on conversation practitioners and the Socratic midwife image.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed with page references in two discussion guides. Coherent and consistent with coaching practice, but presented without empirical testing.

insights.name: Ask for the story, not the summary
insights.explanation: People make sense of who they are through the stories they tell about their lives, and most rarely get asked to tell them. Brooks describes Dan McAdams's life-story interviews, in which people talk through the high points, low points and turning points of their lives, and many find it moving and are glad to have been asked. He urges switching into narrative mode: instead of asking what someone thinks about something, ask how they came to think it, or ask about the person who most shaped their values. Pay attention to how people frame their story (for example, whether it is a story of redemption), not only to the facts. He adds that in asking, you help the person shape a more coherent account of themselves.
insights.when_to_use: Getting to know a new teammate, interviewing, reconnecting with older relatives, deepening a friendship or romantic relationship, or writing a tribute or introduction for someone.
insights.worked_example: Before introducing a guest speaker, an events coordinator asks her not for her bio but how she ended up in climate finance. The story about a failed first startup becomes the heart of a much better introduction. At a holiday gathering, a grandson asks his grandmother what her first job was like and how she ended up in the city, and hears stories nobody in the family had recorded.
common_mistakes: Asking for facts (where, when, what title) instead of how and why.
Interrupting the story to relate it to yourself.
Judging how someone frames their story instead of being curious about why they frame it that way.
steps: Ask a 'how did you come to' or 'what was that like' question, or ask about a high point, low point or turning point.
Let them take the time to tell it; resist redirecting.
Notice turning points and how they interpret them.
Ask about one turning point in more depth.
Reflect back what the story tells you about what they value.
situations: Getting to know a new teammate

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 3, Chapter 15 'Life Stories' (pp. 212 to 227).
source.underlying_research: Dan P. McAdams, narrative identity research and the life-story interview (confirmed via a review describing Brooks's account of McAdams's sessions). Reader notes also mention identity statuses and imago in the chapter. Whether Brooks discusses contamination sequences specifically was not verified; summaries say he discusses redemption stories.

insights.confidence_rationale: McAdams's role in the chapter is now confirmed. Narrative identity is a substantial research program, but turning it into conversational technique is Brooks's application rather than tested advice.

insights.name: Serving a friend in despair: presence over fixing
insights.explanation: When someone is in deep suffering such as depression, the instinct is to advise, cheer up, or remind them of everything good in their life. Brooks, writing about his oldest friend Peter Marks, who died by suicide after years of severe depression, says those moves often backfire: advice signals you do not understand the illness, and what the person lacks is energy rather than ideas. What helps more is steady presence, acknowledging how bad it is without trying to argue them out of it, staying the same friend you have always been, and many small touches (texts, visits, notes). He also warns against assuming your own sad moments let you understand clinical depression.
insights.when_to_use: A friend, family member or colleague going through depression, grief, serious illness or a long crisis. Not a substitute for professional help when there is risk of self-harm.
insights.worked_example: A coworker returns from leave after her brother's death and is withdrawn. Rather than offering grief books or saying it will get better, her teammate sends a short message every few days ('thinking of you, no need to reply'), invites her to the usual Friday walk, and when she talks, says 'that sounds unbearable' instead of trying to reframe it. In a family case, a son whose father is depressed after retirement stops sending him lists of hobbies to try and instead comes over to watch the game every Sunday as they used to.
common_mistakes: Offering solutions or self-help tips to someone who lacks the energy to act on them.
Trying to cheer them up by pointing to their blessings, which can make them feel more alone.
Saying you understand because you have felt down too.
Disappearing because you do not know what to say.
Not taking risk signs seriously; presence complements professional care, it does not replace it.
steps: Show up and keep showing up; consistency matters more than eloquence.
Acknowledge the reality of their pain without minimizing or reframing it.
Hold back advice unless asked; ask what would help, if anything.
Keep being your ordinary self with them; normal company is a gift.
Send small, low-pressure touches that require no reply.
If you notice risk of self-harm, encourage professional help and contact crisis resources.
situations: Parent struggling after retirement or diagnosis

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 10 'How Do You Serve a Friend Who Is in Despair?' (pp. 122 to 133), adapted from his NYT essay 'How Do You Serve a Friend in Despair?' (February 2023).
source.underlying_research: Primarily Brooks's own experience with Peter Marks. He reports reading later that advice to a depressed person often signals you do not understand; no specific study confirmed. The advice is broadly consistent with mainstream guidance for supporters, which is outside the book.

insights.confidence_rationale: Content confirmed via a blog quoting the chapter and reader notes: his job was not to cheer his friend up but to acknowledge the reality and keep showing up, and he wished he had sent more small touches. Rests on a single, deeply considered personal case, so flagged. Rated Medium because the core advice aligns with widely accepted clinical and peer-support guidance. Timeline: the chapter places the visible onset of Marks's depression in spring 2019; the earlier note that a secondary source dated his death to 2019 reflects this confusion.

insights.name: Empathy as three trainable skills: mirror, mentalize, care
insights.explanation: Brooks breaks empathy into three parts: mirroring (picking up and accurately reading another person's emotions), mentalizing (working out why they feel that way, using your own experience as a rough guide), and caring (actually wanting good things for them and acting on it). He stresses that people differ in natural empathy but everyone improves with practice. Combined with the perspective-getting finding, the practical lesson is to notice the emotion, check your read by asking, and then show concern through action.
insights.when_to_use: When someone's reaction surprises you, when delivering bad news, managing a stressed team, or supporting a partner whose feelings you do not immediately understand.
insights.worked_example: A team lead notices a normally chatty designer has gone quiet in standups (mirroring). She guesses it might be the new review process making him feel micromanaged, but rather than assume, she asks privately how the change has landed (mentalizing, with checking). He says it is actually a sick parent. She offers flexible hours for the month (caring). The same three moves help a partner who notices her husband's irritability before a family wedding.
common_mistakes: Stopping at mirroring: feeling their distress without understanding or helping.
Mentalizing purely by projection and never checking the guess.
Caring in the way you would want rather than the way they need.
steps: Notice: name to yourself the emotion you are picking up.
Hypothesize why, but treat it as a guess.
Check by asking an open question.
Respond with a concrete act of care that fits what they said they need.
situations: Partner stressed before a family event

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 11 'The Art of Empathy' (pp. 134 to 159), which also covers defenses that make people hard to know (drawing on Will Storr's 'sacred flaw') and ways to build empathy such as contact, literature and finer emotion labeling; Chapter 12 'How Were You Shaped by Your Sufferings?' (p. 160) on hardship and empathy.
source.underlying_research: Matches the standard split of empathy into affective resonance, cognitive perspective and empathic concern. Brooks links mentalizing to Adam Smith's projective view of sympathy. Specific empirical studies he cites in this chapter were not verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Three-part breakdown confirmed in reader notes. It mirrors mainstream academic models of empathy, and trainability has some research support. Brooks describes mentalizing as drawing on your own memories, which the perspective-getting research suggests should be checked by asking, as the steps here do.

insights.name: Hard conversations: tend the actual conversation, not just the official one
insights.explanation: Brooks says every conversation runs on two levels: the official one about the topic, and the actual one carried by the feelings flowing underneath, where each remark makes the other person feel a little safer or a little more threatened. So in a hard conversation, think about conditions before content: set up safety and trust before getting into the substance. Notice the frame of the conversation, and do not shift it away when the other person is trying to say something painful or important. Avoid labeling (dismissing someone by tying them to a group). Use splitting: name the differences, then find the thing you share and build from there. He also stresses that people from different social positions experience different worlds, so acknowledging their experience can matter more than winning the point.
insights.when_to_use: When a discussion with a relative, colleague or friend escalates; in cross-functional disputes; during political conversations at family gatherings; in tense performance discussions.
insights.worked_example: Two department heads are arguing about budget cuts and voices are rising. One notices that the real conversation has become about whether her peer feels his team is being treated as expendable, so she says: 'Before we get into numbers, I want to be clear I am not saying your team matters less. We both want to keep the client renewals. Can we start from there?' At a holiday dinner, a daughter whose uncle starts describing how his small business was hurt by a policy resists turning it into a debate about statistics, and asks what that period was like for him.
common_mistakes: Arguing the official topic while ignoring the feelings underneath.
Jumping to substance before there is enough trust to hear it.
Changing the frame (to logistics, to your own story) when the other person raises something painful.
Labeling the other person instead of engaging what they said.
Expecting one conversation to resolve a deep disagreement.
steps: Before the content, set conditions: a private setting, enough time, and a signal of goodwill.
Track the actual conversation: is what you just said making them feel safer or more threatened?
If they raise something painful, stay in their frame instead of steering back to your point.
Avoid labels; describe what they said, not what group it puts them in.
Split: name the difference clearly, then name what you share, and build from the shared point.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 9 'Hard Conversations' (pp. 107 to 121): conditions before content (p. 112), two levels of conversation (p. 114), frames (p. 115), splitting (p. 117).
source.underlying_research: Reviewers say the chapter draws on the difficult-conversations literature. The two-level idea resembles the 'feelings conversation' in Stone, Patton and Heen's Difficult Conversations, but no source read shows Brooks citing them. The original first-pass move of stepping back to ask how the conversation got so tense came from one review that could not be re-read (Medium returned 403) and was not found in any other source, so it was replaced by the confirmed content.

insights.confidence_rationale: Chapter content now confirmed with page references. The approach is consistent with established conflict-resolution practice, but Brooks's specific tools are presented without tests and the step sequence is a synthesis. Kept Low.

insights.name: Read the energy and the life chapter, not the type
insights.explanation: In Part 3, Brooks offers two lenses for understanding someone more fully. First, personality as the energy someone brings into a room: he favors the research-based Big Five (extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, agreeableness, openness) over Myers-Briggs, which he dismisses, and stresses that traits can change, with people generally becoming more agreeable, conscientious and emotionally stable with age. Second, life tasks: a sequence of developmental challenges that can continue throughout life rather than in fixed stages, which he lists as the imperial task (proving competence), the interpersonal task (fitting in and belonging), career consolidation (becoming really good at something), the generative task (serving the next generation), and integrity versus despair in old age. Knowing which task someone is in the middle of tells you what kind of conversation and support they need. He treats both as prompts for attention, not boxes.
insights.when_to_use: Managing people at different career stages, mentoring, understanding why a parent or partner is changing, adapting communication style to a quiet versus outgoing colleague.
insights.worked_example: A manager has two reports: a 26-year-old eager to prove herself and a 58-year-old veteran who has become more interested in training others. Instead of offering both the same stretch project, she gives the younger one a high-visibility deliverable and asks the veteran to design onboarding. At home, a man realizes his recently retired father's new fixation on family history is about meaning and legacy, and starts asking him about it rather than teasing him.
common_mistakes: Typecasting people from a quiz result or a stage label.
Using Myers-Briggs as if it were a reliable predictor.
Assuming age determines life task; people reach these at different times.
situations: Managing reports at different career stages
Adapting to introverted or extraverted colleagues

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 3, Chapter 13 'Personality: What Energy Do You Bring into the Room?' (pp. 175 to 189; Big Five pp. 179 to 186; personality change p. 189) and Chapter 14 'Life Tasks' (pp. 190 to 211).
source.underlying_research: Big Five (Five-Factor) model; Brooks quotes Roberts and Yoon's 2022 review that personality, especially neuroticism, changes with intervention (Annual Review of Psychology). Life tasks: Erikson (integrity versus despair, generativity); 'imperial' and 'interpersonal' are Robert Kegan's terms, and a study-guide summary says Brooks draws on Kegan (not confirmed from the book); 'career consolidation' is George Vaillant's term, not confirmed as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: The Big Five and evidence for trait change are high-confidence research; stage and task models are more contested and descriptive. Using either as a conversational lens is Brooks's application and untested as a communication technique.

insights.name: You read people less accurately than you think
insights.explanation: Brooks opens with a humbling claim: most of us are much worse at reading others than we believe. He cites William Ickes's empathic-accuracy research, in which strangers in a first conversation correctly infer each other's thoughts only a small fraction of the time and close friends and family do only somewhat better, while people who read others poorly tend to think they are as good as the accurate ones. He adds that long-term partners can lock in an early picture of each other and stop updating it, which he calls the static mindset, and that we assume other people's inner lives are simpler than our own (Epley's lesser-minds problem). The practical lesson is humility: treat your read of someone as a guess, and keep updating it.
insights.when_to_use: Before acting on an assumption about what someone thinks or feels: a partner of many years, a parent, a long-time colleague, a new hire, or anyone you feel sure you have figured out.
insights.worked_example: A manager has worked with the same analyst for six years and assumes he still wants no part of client work, because he said so early on. Before staffing a new account, she asks him instead of deciding for him, and learns he has been hoping for client exposure for a year. At home, a man who has been married for twenty years catches himself predicting his wife's reaction to a holiday plan and asks her what she actually wants this year.
common_mistakes: Equating long familiarity with accurate understanding.
Treating confidence in your read as evidence that it is correct.
Assuming other people's motives are simpler or lower than your own.
Never revisiting an early impression after people change.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, Chapter 1 'The Power of Being Seen' (Ickes findings, around pp. 14 to 15) and Chapter 2 'How Not to See a Person' (lesser-minds problem and static mindset, pp. 20 to 22). Confirmed in the publisher sample.
source.underlying_research: William Ickes's empathic-accuracy research (for example Ickes, Empathic Accuracy, Guilford, 1997; Everyday Mind Reading, Prometheus, 2003). Brooks reports roughly 20 percent accuracy for strangers, 35 percent for friends and family, and about 55 percent for the best readers. The claim that accuracy declines with marriage length rests on limited studies and should be treated as tentative. Nicholas Epley on the lesser-minds problem (Mindwise, 2014).

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book text. Empathic accuracy is an established research paradigm and modest accuracy levels are a consistent finding, but the specific percentages depend on the task and sample, and the marriage-length finding is thinly replicated. The overconfidence point converges with Epley's work.

research_notes: Network policy blocked WebFetch for every non-allowlisted host I tried (zhurnaly.com, conorneill.com, www.mickmel.com all failed DNS resolution), so after three failures I stopped fetching and worked from WebSearch result syntheses only. Those syntheses drew on: Colgate news report of a Brooks talk; Joe Moran's review; Common Reader (Washington University) review; a church discussion guide PDF (squarespace) quoting Chapter 6 page references; SuperSummary chapter pages; Medium summaries; reviews by Bernie Gourley and others; commentary on Brooks's NYT essay 'How Do You Serve a Friend in Despair?' (Feb 2023); APA and Chicago Booth press releases on Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2021/2022); ScienceDaily and Greater Good coverage of Eyal, Steffel and Epley (2018); Penguin Random House and library catalog listings for metadata. I did not read the book text, the Penguin UK sample PDF, the NYT essays themselves, or the podcast interviews (Kate Bowler, RNZ, WHYY, The One You Feed) directly. Verified: Illuminators vs Diminishers; Chapter 4 'Accompaniment'; Chapter 6 'Good Talks' (attention as on/off switch, midwife image, joint exploration); Chapter 7 'The Right Questions' (crossroads-type questions); looping (mentioned in multiple summaries); Chapter 9 'Hard Conversations'; Chapter 10 on Peter Marks; Chapter 11 'The Art of Empathy' (mirroring, mentalizing, caring); Chapter 12 on suffering; Chapter 13 personality (Big Five over Myers-Briggs); Chapter 14 'Life Tasks'; Chapter 15 'Life Stories' (McAdams). The 'Essential Skills for Being Human' piece appears to be an NYT column (Oct 19, 2023), not an Atlantic essay; I found no Atlantic adaptation. Not verified: the exact wording of Brooks's sample questions, specific tips some summaries list ('favor familiarity', 'don't fear the pause', 'don't be a topper'), whom Brooks credits for looping, whether he cites Stone/Patton/Heen or Kegan or McAdams's redemption sequences, and the exact attribution of SLANT. The Eyal et al. participant count (about 2,600) comes from a single secondary source. Some search results were low-quality AI-generated pages (presentationbuilder.internationaltrucks.com and similar) and were ignored. Chapter numbering differs slightly across summaries; numbers given here follow the most consistent sources. VERIFICATION PASS (2026-11-04): pages were fetched with curl and read directly; see the verification object. The book text itself was read only in the publisher sample (front matter, contents, Chapters 1 and 2). Later chapters were checked through two church discussion guides with US page references, Blair Nangle's and Derek Sivers's chapter notes, blogs that quote the book (risewithdrew.com), a Temple Emanuel sermon summarizing Brooks on McAdams, Joe Moran's and the Common Reader reviews, and commentary on the NYT essay. Paywalled NYT pages and copies of paywalled study guides were not used. The PubMed abstracts and the author-hosted PDF of Eyal, Steffel and Epley were read.
